newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialist win would not derail EMU -analysts.
newsitem.headline: French Socialist win would not derail EMU -analysts.

text.p: A Socialist victory in France's snap election would be unlikely to derail monetary union but French markets could face turmoil until the new administration's policies became clear, economists said on Friday.
"They (the Socialists) may want a softer EMU (economic and monetary union) but it's quite unlikely they have any idea of abandoning it," said ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard.

After a raft of polls predicting a comfortable victory for the ruling centre-right, a new survey on Thursday suggested the race could be wide open, forecasting the coalition would get only a wafer-thin majority in the 577-seat national assembly.
The IPSOS poll suggested the conservatives would win 292 seats, the Socialists 256, the Communists 28 and the far-right National Front one.

Another poll published on Friday showed a majority of voters believed conservative President Jacques Chirac had failed to honour most of his campaign promises, including his hallmark pledge to roll back unemployment, now at a record 12.8 percent. Market reaction to the polls was relatively muted with bond and stock prices slightly lower. Ten-year bond futures fell only only 0.34 basis points to 128.28 while the franc remained fairly firm against the mark at 3.3760.

The markets were still fairly confident the centre-right would win, traders said. But they were on red alert for more polls and any confirmation that the Socialists had gained ground would be bearish with shorter-dated French government debt taking most of the impact.
"We are going to live and breathe opinion polls," until the two-round vote on May 25 and June 1," said Iain Lindsay of Credit Lyonnais. "It's going to be a bouncy ride."

While some commentators have hailed the boldness of Chirac's move to call the vote nine months ahead of schedule to clear the way for more austerity to ensure France qualifies for monetary union, others say it is a gamble that could backfire. "It's a serious game of poker," said Lindsay.

Several economists also say the vote could become a risky referendum on monetary union. Many voters see EMU as responsible for France's economic woes because of the government belt-tightening required to achieve it. The single currency was approved by only the barest of margins in a 1992 referendum.

But if the Socialists came to power "they cannot pretend it (the Maastricht treaty) was something they inherited from the conservatives," said Steven Englander of Smith Barney in Paris. "I don't think when push comes to shove they can walk away."

It was the Socialists under the late French president Francois Mitterrand who approved the Maastricht treaty. "A large majority of the Socialist electorate is in favour of EMU and (Socialist leader) Lionel Jospin himself has always been so," Eric Chaney of Morgan Stanley said.

Jospin's platform opposes further fiscal restraint to meet the Maastricht criteria and stresses the need to include Italy in the first wave of entrants. His other proposals include a shorter working week without pay cuts and a plan to shift the tax burden from employee income to capital income.

If he becomes prime minister, Jospin "would probably pursue EMU plans," said Jean-Francois Mercier of Salomon Brothers. "He has repeatedly rejected pressure from the party's left wing to endorse an EMU delay."
However, Mercier said the need to maintain the electoral alliance with the Communist Party would mean that a pro-EMU strategy would not take shape until after the election.
Philippe Ithurbide of Societe Generale said there was no doubt, however, that if the Socialists came to power, the "unity of the Franco-German 'couple' would be a little bit weaker."

The market upside to a decisive conservative win could be considerable. "If the coalition gets back in with a 50 seat majority, that puts them in an incredibly powerful position," said Lindsay. "They would have five years to implement their plans. They could transform France in that time."

The centre-right would also be in the happy situation of embarking on talks leading to monetary union unchallenged domestically and be able to implement the tough public spending measures necessary to keep down France's budget deficit.
